You're right, and the reasoning for this is rather simple.

The "/u/" syntax was a sister to the "/r/" syntax on Reddit - that is, any series of characters that can be appended to the basic "reddit.com" URL and still parse correctly would be shortened as a link if you just typed those characters. Hence /r/subreddit linking to reddit.com/r/subreddit, /u/user linking to reddit.com/u/user, etc.

A logical extension from that is typing those characters when you just want to get to that URL without any additional functionality - this is why, for example, /r/undelete/new actually does link to Undelete's new feed. In users, this means that /u/user is at its basic form a link to reddit.com/u/user FIRST and a 'summoning' of user SECOND. @, on the other hand, is borrowed from Twitter, where the first and ONLY purpose of the character is to summon the user listed after the at sign. You can't type in 'voat.co/@user', that doesn't make any sense, so in saying @user you're explicitly saying that you want to summon that user to the discussion.

 

I myself will continue to use /u/ syntax as I find it easier to read in a prose-styled post such as on voat, but the logic for using the at sign instead is still very sound and I respect the differences of those who use the various styles.

What if the German Empire won World War 1?

I would imagine Russia still would have fell to communism, however whether or not the German Empire would have intervened after the war is hard to say. I can say for sure Eastern Europe would look much different as Germany would have propped up Austria-Hungary's expansion into the Balkans. Greece and Bulgaria would likely have been the only countries to still exist in the Balkans with Greece likely losing some turf to Turkey.

I don't know enough about Western Europe to comment, but essentially Austria and Germany would likely have had free reign up to the Urals.

I think the most interesting thing is that, at least assuming they weren't immediately overthrown from within, we'd consider many of the winning group's beliefs "normal." Slavery, as an example, lasted for hundreds of years and arguably was ended in large part not because of a greater moral awakening but because the industrial revolution stripped away much of their value. By comparison in today's society we think it's acceptable for people to live mediocre lives or even go homeless (which is effectively tantamount to being sentenced to an early death) because they fail at capitalism. If the German Empire won we'd mostly be engaged in "normal" behavior and thought of all sorts while occasionally pondering, "What if the allied forces (who certainly would have a different name attached to them) won World War 1?"
